name: Sandalwood

card.summary: A creamy, woody fragrance base note and skincare botanical that people use for scent and, in some products, for skin and hair care.
card.note: Sandalwood oil is a recognised contact allergen at high concentrations.

quick.overview:
Sandalwood is the fragrant heartwood of trees in the genus Santalum, distilled into an oil whose smooth, creamy, woody scent is a staple base note in perfume. For looks, the payoff is mainly olfactory: a lasting scent that is part of grooming. It also appears in skincare products, and a related synthetic sandalwood-like molecule has been studied for hair.

Research is small. A randomized trial studied the synthetic odorant Sandalore for telogen effluvium hair shedding, an acne regimen study included sandalwood oil, and reviews describe the oil's properties in dermatology.
quick.how: People wear sandalwood-based fragrances, use sandalwood soaps and incense, or apply products containing the oil or its synthetic analogues. In traditional practice, sandalwood paste is applied on the skin in South Asian rituals.
quick.risks: Reviews of essential oil contact allergy list sandalwood among oils causing more than 2 percent positive patch-test reactions in tested patients, mostly from pure or high-concentration products. Natural Santalum album is also threatened by over-harvesting.

lead: Sandalwood is the heartwood of trees of the genus Santalum, whose steam-distilled oil has a soft, warm, creamy woody scent that perfumers use as a long-lasting base note and fixative [1][8]. Its main components are the santalol isomers, alpha- and beta-santalol, which together make up the bulk of the oil [8][9].

For appearance, sandalwood works mainly as a fragrance and grooming ingredient: people wear it as perfume, use it in soaps and incense, and find it in some skincare products. A 2017 review describes sandalwood album oil as a botanical for dermatology, noting trials in acne, psoriasis, eczema, warts and molluscum contagiosum [2]. An open-label study evaluated a salicylic acid regimen containing Australian sandalwood oil for mild-to-moderate acne [3].

A randomized, placebo-controlled trial of 60 women examined Sandalore, a synthetic sandalwood-like odorant that activates the olfactory receptor OR2AT4 in hair follicles, in telogen effluvium; the authors reported less shedding and more hair volume than placebo [4]. The trial concerns the synthetic molecule rather than natural sandalwood oil [4][8].

angle.text: Sandalwood is worn as scent and used in soaps and creams. A synthetic analogue has also been tested for hair shedding.

infobox: Alpha- and beta-santalol (about 90 percent of oil is sesquiterpene alcohols) [8]

paras: True sandalwoods are hemiparasitic trees native to Southeast Asia, Melanesia, Australia and the Pacific. The genus has more than 19 species; the main cultivated species, Santalum album, is threatened, and oil from Indian trees commands higher prices because of higher alpha-santalol content [1].

The wood keeps its fragrance for decades. It is sacred in Hinduism and Ayurveda and is used in many religious practices [1]. Trees flower after about seven years, develop fragrance after about ten, and are ready to harvest after about twenty [7]. Other woods sold as red, false or African sandalwood belong to different plant groups and lack the santalol profile of true sandalwood, according to Grokipedia [11].

Sesquiterpene alcohols make up over 90 percent of the oil, with alpha-santalol roughly 50 to 60 percent and beta-santalol about 20 to 25 percent; composition varies with species, region, tree age and extraction method, and ISO 3518:2002 specifies 41 to 55 percent alpha- and 16 to 24 percent beta-santalol for S. album oil [8]. Australian S. spicatum oil has a different, lower santalol profile [1][7].

The oil is made by steam distillation of chips and billets from the heartwood, a process Wikipedia says takes 14 to 36 hours [1][8]. Wikipedia reports that the first essential-oil extraction took place in Mysore in 1917 and that Givaudan attempted synthesis in 1947 [7].

Wikipedia describes S. album as spread by Austronesian traders and naturalised in South India by at least 1300 BCE, and reports use in Indian temple construction, Chinese statues and censers, Egyptian embalming and Muslim funerals [1][7]. Three Hawaiian species were exploited from 1790 to 1825 until supply ran out, and sandalwood was Western Australia's biggest export earner in the 1840s [1].

Indian production fell from about 4,000 tonnes per year in the 1960s to about 350 tonnes in 2014, according to Wikipedia, and India has banned the export of sandalwood timber [7]. Australia overtook India as the largest S. album producer in the 21st century; plantation operators there later ran into financial difficulty, with Quintis entering receivership in 2024 [1][7]. Wikipedia cites prices of about US$2,500 per kilogram for Indian oil and US$1,500 for Australian oil in 2020 [1].

Perfumers use it as a base note in oriental, woody, fougere, chypre and floral-oriental fragrances [1]. Base notes are the heavy, slowly evaporating components that emerge during the dry-down and can remain detectable for many hours; many act as fixatives that hold lighter notes in place [10]. Because natural oil is expensive, synthetic alternatives such as Sandalore, Bacdanol, Ebanol and Brahmanol are widely used [8].

Sandalwood album oil has been reviewed as a botanical agent in dermatology for anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial and anti-proliferative properties [2]. An open-label study used a regimen that included sandalwood oil [3]. The synthetic odorant Sandalore was studied in people with telogen effluvium [4]. Wikipedia says Sandalore and Brahmanol act on the skin receptor OR2AT4 while natural sandalwood oil did not show this effect [8].
Traditional uses include sandalwood paste applied to the skin in South Asian rituals and Ayurvedic use of the oil for conditions such as colds, fever and inflammation [1][8].

A review of essential oil contact allergy lists sandalwood among nine oils with over 2 percent positive patch-test reactions; most reactions come from pure oils or high-concentration products [5]. Wikipedia says the scientific literature documents no significant adverse effects but that safety research is limited, and that the oil is regarded as safe at food-flavouring levels [8].

A 24-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 60 women with telogen effluvium compared 1 percent Sandalore with a similar-smelling placebo oil that does not activate OR2AT4; the authors reported reduced shedding, higher hair volume and a higher share of anagen follicles than placebo, with most of the anti-shedding effect by week 8, and called it proof of principle [4].

An 8-week open-label study of a regimen combining salicylic acid with highly purified Australian sandalwood oil in 47 people with mild-to-moderate facial acne reported that 42 met the primary endpoint on a global aesthetic improvement scale, with mostly mild side effects peaking at week 2; the authors called for longer studies [3].

A randomized trial in healthy adults, who wore masks to exclude smell, examined absorption of East Indian sandalwood oil and alpha-santalol through the skin; the authors interpreted alpha-santalol as producing a relaxing or sedative physiological effect [6].

lore.intro: Sandalwood appears in grooming discussion mainly as a fragrance note and, since the hair-follicle receptor findings, as a talking point about scent and hair; a 2018 Hacker News post carried the headline that a whiff of sandalwood makes the head sprout more hair [12].

claims.believers: The headline circulated in tech discussion that a sandalwood-like scent stimulates hair follicles [12].
claims.experts: The trial used topically applied synthetic Sandalore, and Wikipedia says natural sandalwood oil did not show the same receptor effect [4][8].

claims.believers: Dermatology reviewers cite anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial properties [2].
claims.experts: The acne study was open-label and tested a multi-product regimen, and its authors called for longer studies [3].

claims.claim: Sandalwood is a gentle, low-risk scent
claims.believers: Wikipedia notes the oil is regarded as safe at food-flavouring levels [8].
claims.experts: A contact allergy review lists sandalwood among oils with over 2 percent positive patch tests, mostly from pure or high-concentration products [5].

claims.claim: Skin-applied sandalwood has a calming effect
claims.believers: Aromatherapy practice attributes relaxation to the oil [1].
claims.experts: A randomized trial with masked smell reported physiological sedation from alpha-santalol [6].
